By way of the present appeal under Section 374 of The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (hereinafter referred to as 'Cr.P.C'), the appellant has assailed the impugned judgment dated 20.01.2020 and order on sentence dated 03.03.2025 passed by the court of Ld. JMFC-05, East District, Karkardooma Courts, Delhi in CC No. 1852/2016, FIR No. 243/2007, Police Station Krishna Nagar titled as State v. Santosh Kumar, whereby appellant was AKASH Digitally signed by AKASH JAIN JAIN Date: 2025.09.04 17:26:30 +0530 convicted for the offences under Sections 279/304-A/338 Indian Penal Code, 1860 (hereinafter referred to as 'IPC') and was sentenced to undergo simple imprisonment for a period of 1 month for offence under Section 279 IPC, to undergo simple imprisonment for a period of 1 year for offence under Section 338 IPC and to also undergo simple imprisonment for a period of 1 year for offence under Section 304-A IPC.
All the punishments were ordered to run concurrently and benefit of Section 428 Cr.P.C. was also given to the appellant.

2. During the course of arguments of present appeal, the appellant/ convict and his Counsel submitted that appellant does not wish to assail the impugned judgment dated 20.01.2020 and present appeal be treated as withdrawn only with respect to impugned judgment dated 20.01.2020.
However, he assailed the impugned order on sentence dated 03.03.2025 on mercy grounds.

It is argued that appellant has a wife, two minor children and is sole bread earner of his family.
It is argued that appellant is remorseful of his act and after the incident in question he stopped driving commercial vehicles and started working as labourer to make both ends meet.
It is argued that the appellant belongs to poor strata of society and if he is sent to jail there would be none to look after his family.

It is further argued Digitally signed by AKASH JAIN AKASH JAIN Date: 2025.09.04 17:26:36 +0530 that appellant/convict had already spent 6 days in custody in this case and may be awarded benefit of probation.
4. Per contra, it is argued by Ld. Addl. PP for the State that order on sentence dated 03.03.2025 is just, reasonable and does not suffer from any legal infirmity.

It is further argued that at the time of alleged incident in question the appellant was driving a blue line bus in rash and negligent manner and hit one stationary motor-cycle from the back which was standing at a red light being driven by complainant/ injured Kunwar Singh causing grievous injury to him and further causing death of his wife who was the pillion rider and got crushed under the tyres of offending blue line bus.
5.

During the course of proceedings, complainant/ respondent no. 2 Kunwar Singh had also appeared and stated that he had lost his wife in the alleged incident in question and also suffered fracture in his hand, as such, suitable punishment maybe given to the appellant as per law.
He further stated that he did not want any compensation from the appellant or the State.

6. In Dhananjoy Chatterjee v. State of W. B., (1994) 2 SCC 220, while discussing the aspect of adequate sentencing, Hon'ble Supreme Court of India was pleased to hold as following:-
".... 14.

sentences.text: In recent years, the rising crime rate particularly violent crime against women has made the criminal sentencing by the courts a subject of concern.
Today AKASH Digitally signed by AKASH JAIN JAIN Date: 2025.09.04 17:26:41 +0530 there are admitted disparities.

Some criminals get very harsh sentences while many receive grossly different sentence for an essentially equivalent crime and a shockingly large number even go unpunished thereby encouraging the criminal and in the ultimate making justice suffer by weakening the system's credibility.

Of course, it is not possible to lay down any cut and dry formula relating to imposition of sentence but the object of sentencing should be to see that the crime does not go unpunished and the victim of crime as also the society has the satisfaction that justice has been done to it.

In imposing sentences in the absence of specific legislation, Judges must consider variety of factors and after considering all those factors and taking an overall view of the situation, impose sentence which they consider to be an appropriate one.
Aggravating factors cannot be ignored and similarly mitigating circumstances have also to be taken into consideration.

15. In our opinion, the measure of punishment in a given case must depend upon the atrocity of the crime; the conduct of the criminal and the defenceless and unprotected Santosh Kumar Singh vs State on 4 September, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/6364126/
2 state of the victim.

sentences.text: Imposition of appropriate punishment is the manner in which the courts respond to the society's cry for justice against the criminals.
Justice demands that courts should impose punishment befitting the crime so that the courts reflect public abhorrence of the crime.
The courts must not only keep in view the rights of the criminal but also the rights of the victim of crime and the society at large while considering imposition of appropriate punishment...."

7. Further, in the case of Mahesh v. State of M.P., (1987) 3 SCC 80, Hon'ble Apex Court had observed that:-
"... We also feel that it will be a mockery of justice to permit these appellants to escape the extreme penalty of law when faced with such evidence and such cruel acts.
To give the lesser punishment for the appellants would be to render the justicing system of this country suspect.

sentences.text: The common man will lose faith in courts.
In such cases, he understands and appreciates the language of deterrence more than the reformative jargon.
When we say this, we do not ignore the need for a reformative AKASH Digitally signed by AKASH JAIN JAIN Date: 2025.09.04 17:26:46 +0530 approach in the sentencing process...."

8. While specifically dealing with the menace of blue line buses it was held by Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in the case of Dalbir Singh v. State of Haryana, AIR 2000 SC 1677 that criminal courts cannot treat nature of offence under Section 304A IPC as attracting the benevolent provisions of Section 4 of The Probation of Offfenders Act.

sentences.text:
The relevant excerpt of the judgment is reproduced as under:-
"....

Bearing in mind the galloping trend in road accidents in India and the devastating consequences visiting the victims and their families, criminal courts cannot treat the nature of the offence under Section 304- A IPC as attracting the benevolent provisions of Section 4 of the P.O. Act.
While considering the quantum of sentence, to be imposed for the offence of causing death by rash or negligent driving of automobiles, one of the prime consid-erations should be deterrence.
A professional driver pedals the accelerator of the automobile almost throughout his working hours.
He must constantly inform himself that he cannot afford to have a single moment of laxity or inattentiveness when his leg is on the pedal of a vehicle in locomotion.

He cannot and should not take a chance think that a rash driving need not necessarily cause any accident; or even if any accident occurs it need not necessarily result in the death of any human being; or even if such death ensues he might not be convicted of the offence; and lastly that even if he is convicted he would be dealt with leniently by the court.
He must always keep in his mind the fear psyche that if he is convicted of the offence for causing death of a human being due to his callous driving of vehicle he cannot escape from jail sentence.

This is the role which the courts can play,
particularly at the level of trial courts, for lessening the high rate of motor accidents due to callous driving of automobiles...."

Now, Section 386 Cr.P.C. provides for the powers of the Appellate Court in an appeal which stipulates as under:
AKASH Digitally signed by AKASH JAIN JAIN Date: 2025.09.04 17:26:51 +0530 Section 386 Cr.P.C:- Powers of Appellate Court "....

After perusing such record and hearing the appellant or his pleader, if he appears, and the Public Prosecutor, if he appears, and in case of an appeal under section 377 or section 378, the accused, if he appears, the Appellate Court may, if it considers that there is no sufficient ground for interfering, dismiss the appeal, or may (a) in an appeal from an order of acquittal, reverse such order and direct that further inquiry be made, or that the accused be re-tried or committed for trial, as the case may be, or find him guilty and pass sentence on him according to law;
(b) in an appeal from a conviction (i) reverse the finding and sentence and acquit or discharge the accused, or order him to be re-tried by a Court of competent jurisdiction subordinate to such Appellate Court or committed for trial, or (ii) alter the finding, maintaining the sentence, or (iii) with or without altering the finding, alter the nature or the extent, or the nature and extent, of the sentence, but not so as to enhance the same;
As already mentioned above, appellant/ convict has not pressed the present appeal on merits and merely pressed for modification of sentence on the ground of mercy.
Normally, the Appellate Court would not interfere in the discretion exercised by the Ld. Trial Court in awarding the sentence or fine.
However, the facts, circumstances as well as the interests of justice demand to revisit the order on point of sentence.
11. As per record, the date of incident is 08.06.2007 and the appellant is facing trial since the year 2008 and has diligently appeared on all the dates fixed by the Court.

It is also noticed that AKASH JAIN Date:

The appellant is further remorseful of his act and stated that the incident in question happened due to accident without any ill intention.

sentences.text: The Court though cannot loose sight of the fact that a precious life was lost in the present accident i.e. wife of complainant Kunwar Singh (who also sustained grievous injury in the accident).

Thus, considering the totality of facts, circumstances, ratio of judgments discussed above and balancing the rights of appellant as well as victim, this Court deems it expedient to not extend the benefit of probation to the present appellant/ convict.

However, while exercising powers under Section 386(b) (iii) Cr.P.C., the sentence is altered to the extent that the appellant/ convict is sentenced to undergo simple imprisonment for a period of one month for offence under Section 279 IPC, to undergo simple imprisonment for a period of 6 months for offence under Section 338 IPC and further undergo simple imprisonment for a period of 8 months for offence under Section 304A IPC.
Benefit of Section 428 Cr.P.C. be also given to the appellant/ convict.

Considering the nature of offences and fact that the appellant/ convict has no means to compensate the victim, a recommendation is made to DLSA, East to award suitable compensation to the victim in the present case under Section 357A of Cr.P.C.
14.
Appellant be taken into custody to serve the sentence and be sent to jail under appropriate warrants.
15. Copy of this judgment along with Trial Court record be sent to the Ld. Trial Court for information.
A copy of the judgment be supplied to appellant free of cost.
16. File be consigned to record room after due compliance.
